blocks.text: Start with a small set of questions before reading.
Mark the exact thing that stopped you: an unknown term, a rule, a calculation, a trace or a choice between alternatives.
Use the question lookup to open the relevant section.
Read one section, close it, and explain the rule in your own words.
Solve the question again and say why each other choice fails.
Then change one assumption or input and solve the variation.
This checks understanding beyond recognition.
A useful 60-minute session: 10 minutes of cold questions, 20 minutes of focused reading, 20 minutes of closed-book solving and 10 minutes updating an error log.
Adjust the timing to your needs.
Revisit mistakes after a gap, for example the next day, several days later and the following week.
These intervals are a practical starting plan, not a fixed learning law.
Record the section ID, your mistaken rule, the corrected rule and one boundary case.
Keep the log short enough to review.
Mix related courses during revision: programming with data structures; databases with security; networking with administration.
Explain how the same word changes meaning across contexts.
Emphasize definitions, key differences, algorithm costs, SDLC models, databases, networking and security.
Use short oral questions to check understanding and correct common misconceptions.
Combine those habits with the tracing, calculation, design and diagnosis demanded by the Ministry learning outcomes.
Allocate revision by both exam share and your error log.
A course with fewer items can still deserve more time if your foundations are weak.
The blueprint is a planning baseline, not a prediction of exact questions.
Definitions: distinguish nearby concepts, not just their names.
Calculations: write units, formulas, assumptions and intermediate steps.
Code and SQL: check validity before tracing the text; state any changes before analyzing a corrected version.
Algorithms and protocols: know the input, decision rule, state change, termination and failure cases.
Design choices: state the criterion.
A choice can change when cost, reliability, consistency or latency matters more.

rows: Reserve extra practice for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP, client/server behavior and safe data handling.
Trace operations and compare their assumptions and costs.
Each of the other fourteen courses
Study all sixteen; do not abandon a whole course based on a short note or an alleged repeated-question list.

title: START03 How to handle exam traps

blocks.text: Underline NOT, FALSE, BEST and EXCEPT before comparing choices.
Check whether the stem supplies enough facts to select one answer.
A long scenario is not automatically an analysis question, and a familiar answer letter is not evidence.
When code is invalid, a diagram is absent, or two choices express the same rule, identify the clarification needed before answering.
Learn the correct rule and the smallest clarification needed.
Do not memorize an arbitrary key as a universal fact.
Distinguish worst case from average case, and an upper bound from a tight bound.
Check language version, SQL dialect, addressing assumptions, graph weights and tie-breaking rules.
For subnetting and scheduling, calculate rather than guess from a familiar number.
Use timed mixed papers only after you can explain your errors.
Revisit the reading sections behind recurring mistakes.
